He just wanted to spear the saboteur through the eye socket with a jagged IV stand and maybe crush a few tiles for good measure. The Entity’s judgment was already burning in the back of his skull — sharp, electric. Her attention stung. Jake’s little stunt with the hook had tipped him further into Her disfavor, and he could feel the leash tightening. One kill. That’s all he needed. Just one — and She might let him breathe again. That was the calculus now. One guaranteed sacrifice to take the edge off the migraine of divine punishment clawing through his thoughts. He could manage that. And on a personal level? The audacity of these survivors was insulting. Hiding instead of playing. No flair. No drama. No fucking respect for the hunt anymore. What was the point of all this if they were just going to cower ? He doubled back to check on his prize, staring for a moment at the discarded handcuffs, empty and swinging gently from their spot on the cabinet. Of course the cop was gone. Of COURSE . He ground his teeth and clenched the baton in his fist hard enough that the current snapped along its length. Three guesses which pest had cut the leash. If he hadn’t diverted toward the last generator’s detonation, hoping to pick someone off mid-flee, he might’ve caught them. A rare lapse in judgment. One he wouldn’t make again. They only had one generator left. And now, all of them were in the same wing. A bottleneck. He could practically feel the survivors trying to creep their way back toward it. Perfect. With deliberate steps, he angled himself toward the final sector, threading through the halls like a wolf circling its cornered prey. This trial wasn’t over yet. And nobody — nobody — was getting out if he had anything to say about it. When Herman entered the central hallway linking the last of the generators, he didn’t expect a roadblock. Yet there Jake stood — centered, unmoving, arms stretched wide across the narrow space as if he were enough to stop a monster. It was such a stupid pose, so mockingly symbolic, that for a split second, Herman nearly burst out laughing. So. The pest was done running. This could be an easy takedown. No thrill, no chase — just a single, cathartic strike to vent his fury and be done with it. But something in his posture, in the look of his eyes, gave Herman pause. Not defiance. Resolve . Not the kind that shouted or bluffed or begged. The quiet kind. The suicidal kind. The kind Herman had seen in soldiers who stopped flinching once the worst outcome became acceptable. That... piqued his curiosity. He came to a stop, eyeing the young man curiously. "I want to make a deal." Well... this was new. Survivors often begged, pleaded, screamed at him to stop. Sometimes they even tried offering the items they brought through the Fog in appeasement. But attempting a bargain? The absurdity of it made Herman cock his head, eyes narrowing with a flicker of amusement. "Audacious, aren't we? What part of this makes you think you are in any position to be making demands ?" Jake fought back a shiver, took a breath to steel himself, prayed the Doctor didn't notice the light tremor in his hands betraying how hard he was working to stand still . “I’m going to help finish the last generator. The girls will leave through the gate unharmed. You’ll send Leon back to the campfire. Through the Entity.” A hook sacrifice. Specifically, the one he had originally been denied. The very same fate Jake had denied his teammate earlier, now offered up like a sacred ritual. Full circle. Poetic. It would be satisfying on principle alone — watching the guilt curdle behind his eyes as he undid his own moral stand — but more than that, it was useful . A hook kill guaranteed his offering. No complications. No escape attempts. No malfunctions. One solid sacrifice to ease the pressure in his skull. Still... He wasn’t in a rush to agree. "I see,” Herman’s tone dripped bitterness. “And what, pray tell, do you offer in exchange for such lavish generosity on my part?” Jake's face hardened. He lowered his arms, trying to straighten his posture, hoping he looked more confident than he felt. "Once the others safely gone, I'll let you send me back to the campfire however you want." A shiver of static surged down Herman’s spine, excitement flaring sharp and visceral before he could even mask it. He inhaled, slow and deliberate, and the charge built in his chest like a thunderhead. Electricity crackled along his arms, climbing his sleeves in visible arcs as it danced across his fingertips. Jake flinched. Just barely. But it was there. The offer had struck its target. A willing sacrifice. No hunt. No chase. No wasted effort on disarming or downing or dragging. Just four full minutes — four — of undisturbed access to a live, consenting subject before the Fog claimed its due. Oh, he could work with that. Now THIS . This was a bargain worth his attention. "If I agree to your terms, what guarantee do I have that you won't simply slip away the moment the gate opens?" Jake blinked, genuinely surprised it had gotten this far. “I mean... you don’t,” he admitted. “Just like I’ve got no guarantee you won’t just capture the others anyways and still kill me for the hell of it.” His mouth was dry, tongue sticking slightly to the roof of it. But he held his ground, forced himself not to waver. “I guess we’d both be taking it on faith.” Jake shifted and held out a hand, his eyes fiercely locked into the Doctor's manic stare, daring him.
